sources.publisher: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis via FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

industries.name: Technology & Semiconductors
industries.notes: Austin's "Silicon Hills" anchors the metro economy. Dell, Apple, Google, Oracle, Tesla, and Samsung all operate major campuses here. IT manufacturing and services averaged around $163,000 in annual earnings per worker in 2023—roughly double the metro average.

industries.name: Government & Public Administration
industries.notes: Austin is the Texas state capital. State agencies, the City of Austin (~15,400 employees), and federal offices make government one of the largest single employment blocks in the metro.

industries.name: Professional & Business Services
industries.notes: Professional and business services account for roughly 20% of metro GDP and saw 5–6% real growth in 2023. The sector covers legal, consulting, finance, and marketing firms that support Austin's large corporate base.

industries.name: Healthcare & Life Sciences
industries.notes: Healthcare employs 7.4% of Austin's workforce, with Ascension Seton (14,000+ staff) and St. David's HealthCare (11,000+ staff) among the metro's top five employers. The Dell Medical School at UT Austin anchors a growing cluster of nearly 300 life sciences companies.

industries.name: Advanced Manufacturing (Semiconductors & EVs)
industries.notes: Semiconductor and EV manufacturing together employ roughly 70,000+ workers in the Austin metro. Samsung, NXP Semiconductors, and Tesla's Giga Texas plant are anchor facilities, driving demand for engineering and production talent.

landmarks.name: Texas State Capitol
landmarks.visualNotes: A 302-foot dome clad in warm sunset-red Texas granite, completed in 1888. The dome is topped by the 16-foot aluminium 'Goddess of Liberty' statue. The building is taller than the US Capitol in Washington, D.C., and sits at the north end of Congress Avenue.

landmarks.name: Ann W. Richards Congress Avenue Bridge
landmarks.visualNotes: A flat concrete arch road bridge, 910 feet long, spanning Lady Bird Lake on the Colorado River in downtown Austin. Unremarkable in daylight, it becomes dramatic at sunset when up to 1.5 million Mexican free-tailed bats stream out from gaps in its concrete underside in a dense, dark ribbon over the water.

landmarks.name: Sixth Street Entertainment District
landmarks.visualNotes: A six-block strip of low-rise 19th-century brick commercial buildings in central Austin, densely lit at night with neon bar signs, string lights, and live-music venue marquees. The street is pedestrianised on weekend evenings, drawing large crowds along its narrow, historically preserved storefronts.

landmarks.name: Barton Springs Pool
landmarks.visualNotes: A spring-fed outdoor swimming pool roughly three acres in size, set inside Zilker Park. The water runs a consistent 68–70°F year-round, fed by natural limestone aquifer springs. Surrounded by pecan trees and open lawn, the pool's concrete dam and stone surrounds sit in a green river valley below downtown's skyline.

landmarks.name: University of Texas Tower (UT Austin Main Building)
landmarks.visualNotes: A 307-foot white limestone tower rising above the UT Austin campus, built in 1937 in a stripped classical style. The tower is illuminated orange at night after major Longhorns victories. It anchors a large Beaux-Arts campus that extends north from the city centre.
